Uppermost
ŭp´ẽr-mōst
adj. (highest in place or rank; the chief seat — Greek protoklisia, the first couch)
From upper and -most. In the Gospels the phrase uppermost rooms renders protoklisia, the first place at table, where the couches were ranked by honour.

Biblical Definition

Uppermost is the highest place, and the Lord Jesus uses it in His indictment of the scribes and Pharisees: they “love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues” (Mat 23:6). The word rendered rooms means the first couch at the table; at an ancient feast the places were ranked, everybody knew the ranking, and the seating was a public statement about a man's standing. The Lord does not object to the existence of order; He objects to the loving of it — a religion whose satisfactions are positional. His own instruction reverses the movement: “when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher” (Luk 14:10). The word appears elsewhere in plain description: the chief baker's dream, “in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head” (Gen 40:17); and Isaiah's picture of desolation, “his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation” (Isa 17:9). The highest branch is the one the gleaners could not reach and the harvesters abandoned — height and emptiness together.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines uppermost as highest in place; highest in power or authority; predominant.

expand to see more

UP'PERMOST, a. Highest in place; as the uppermost seats.

2. Highest in power or authority; predominant; as, ambition was uppermost in his mind.

UP'PER, a. Higher; superior in place; as the upper story.

ROOM, n. Place; space; in the Scriptures, a place at table, as the uppermost rooms at feasts.

Key Scripture

Matthew 23:6 — "And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,"

Luke 14:10 — "But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee."

Isaiah 17:9 — "In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation."

Genesis 40:17 — "And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head."

Modern Corruption

Position within the church is sought and defended as though it were the point of ministry, and the Lord's reversal is admired without being obeyed.

expand to see more

Matthew 23:6 names an appetite, not an office: they love the uppermost rooms. The scribes had real authority and sat in Moses' seat, and the Lord told the people to observe what they said. The sin was the loving — the enjoyment of the position for its own sake, the greetings in the markets, the title. Every generation of the church reproduces it with its own currencies: the platform, the byline, the reputation among peers, the seat at the right table. It is not detected by asking whether a man holds a high place but whether he loves it, and the test appears the moment the place is threatened.

Luke 14:10 is regularly misread as a technique. Sit low and be called higher — a strategy for gaining honour by declining it, which would leave the appetite entirely intact and merely change its method. The Lord closes that reading in the next verse: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. The exalting is God's act and is not extracted by arrangement. And the parable that follows tells the host to invite those who cannot recompense him — the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind — which is the same doctrine applied where no seating chart can flatter anybody.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek protoklisia (G4411), the chief reclining place at a feast — Matthew 23:6, Luke 14:7, Mark 12:39; protokathedria (G4410), the chief seat in the synagogue; Hebrew elyon (H5945), upper, highest.

expand to see more

Greek protoklisia (G4411) — the first couch, chief place at table; Matthew 23:6, Mark 12:39, Luke 14:7-8, Luke 20:46.

Greek protokathedria (G4410) — the chief seat; the companion phrase, of the synagogues.

Hebrew elyon (H5945) — upper, uppermost, and also the divine title Most High.

Hebrew amir (H534) — a topmost bough; Isaiah 17:6 and 17:9.

Luke 14:11 supplies the rule the whole passage rests on: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

Usage

"“Love the uppermost rooms at feasts” — the sin is in the loving."

"“Go and sit down in the lowest room” — and it is not a technique."

"“A forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch” — height and emptiness together."
